name: Splenogonadal fusion
aliases: accessory splenic tissue fused to gonad

reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital anomaly in which splenic tissue is abnormally connected to the gonad or a mesonephric derivative, arising when the splenic anlage lies adjacent to the developing gonad and urogenital ridge in the dorsal mesogastrium during the second month of embryonic development

Two forms are recognised: a continuous type, in which a cord of splenic or fibrous tissue links the orthotopic spleen to the gonad, and a discontinuous type, in which isolated ectopic splenic tissue is fused to the gonad with no connection to the spleen
There is a marked left-sided and male predominance, so the left testis is the structure most often involved
The continuous type is associated with terminal transverse limb defects and micrognathia, constituting the splenogonadal fusion-limb defect syndrome
It typically presents as a scrotal or inguinal mass or an undescended testis and is a well-recognised mimic of a testicular tumour, risking unnecessary orchidectomy
The ectopic splenic tissue enlarges in parallel with the spleen during systemic illness, so the scrotal swelling may wax and wane with intercurrent infection
Because the diagnosis is frequently made only at operation, intra-operative frozen section and radionuclide splenic scintigraphy help confirm splenic tissue and permit testis-sparing surgery
reference.pathophysiology: During the second month of embryogenesis the splenic primordium develops within the dorsal mesogastrium in close proximity to the left urogenital ridge, mesonephros and gonad. If splenic tissue adheres abnormally to the gonadal anlage before the gonad begins its descent, the splenic tissue is either tethered to or carried along with the gonad. In the continuous type a cord, sometimes beaded with splenic nodules, connects the orthotopic spleen to the gonad; in the discontinuous type an isolated mass of splenic tissue is fused to the gonad. The preponderance of left-sided and male cases reflects these embryological relationships, and the association with limb reduction defects in the continuous type reflects the timing of the developmental insult.
additionalDifferentials: Paratesticular rhabdomyosarcoma or other paratesticular tumour
Epididymo-orchitis or torsion of a testicular appendage
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to characterise the mass and its vascularity
Technetium-labelled sulphur colloid or heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy to identify splenic tissue
Serum germ cell tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin, lactate dehydrogenase) to help exclude malignancy
MRI of the pelvis and scrotum for anatomical characterisation
Skeletal and craniofacial assessment for associated limb defects and micrognathia in the continuous type
redFlags: A scrotal mass misinterpreted as malignancy prompting orchidectomy
A hard or rapidly enlarging testicular mass requiring urgent tumour work-up
Associated limb reduction defects or micrognathia indicating the syndromic form
An undescended testis with its attendant malignancy and torsion risk
reference.prognosis: Splenogonadal fusion is benign and the prognosis is excellent when it is recognised and treated with testis-sparing excision of the ectopic splenic tissue. The principal avoidable morbidity is unnecessary orchidectomy resulting from misdiagnosis as a testicular tumour.
pitfalls: Removing the testis for a presumed tumour without frozen section or splenic scintigraphy
Not considering the diagnosis in a boy with a left scrotal mass and a limb anomaly
Attributing a waxing and waning scrotal swelling to a hernia
Failing to preserve the gonad in a child when benign splenic tissue is confirmed
Overlooking associated cryptorchidism and its long-term surveillance needs
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Testis-sparing excision of the ectopic splenic tissue as definitive treatment, preserving the gonad
Avoid unnecessary orchidectomy by recognising the diagnosis and using intra-operative frozen-section histology when a testicular tumour is suspected
Pre-operative confirmation of splenic tissue with scintigraphy and exclusion of malignancy with germ cell tumour markers
Orchidopexy where the anomaly is associated with an undescended testis
Assess for and manage associated terminal transverse limb defects and micrognathia in the continuous type
Paediatric surgery and urology referral, with reassurance regarding the benign nature and excellent prognosis
